content: 1. A study conducted in British Columbia, Canada, evaluated the outcomes of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and its impact on HIV care delivery. 2. Pyne JM and colleagues assessed the effectiveness of collaborative care models for managing depression in HIV clinics, highlighting the importance of mental health integration in HIV care. 3. Mountain E et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine antiretroviral therapy (ART) uptake, adherence, and outcomes among HIV-infected female sex workers, emphasizing the unique challenges faced by this population. 4. Graham SM and colleagues investigated ART adherence and clinical outcomes among young adults engaging in high-risk sexual behaviors, including men who have sex with men, in coastal Kenya. 5. Ford N et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the rates of HIV viral resuppression following elevated viral loads, providing insights into treatment efficacy. 6. Mekuria LA and colleagues compared different adherence measures, such as self-reports, clinician records, and pharmacy refills, to predict detectable viral loads in ART programs without routine plasma viral load monitoring. 7. Hine P et al. reviewed measures of ART adherence to detect viral non-suppression in people living with HIV, offering evidence for improving adherence monitoring. 8. Bisson GP and colleagues compared pharmacy refill adherence with CD4 count changes as monitoring tools for HIV-infected adults on ART, providing evidence for optimizing adherence tracking. 9. Court R et al. demonstrated that short-term adherence tools can predict treatment failure in patients on second-line protease inhibitor-based ART regimens. 10. Henegar CE and colleagues compared pharmacy-based adherence measures as predictors of virological failure in HIV-infected individuals, emphasizing the importance of accurate adherence monitoring. 11. Almeida-Brasil CC et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the predictive performance of various adherence measures for detecting virologic failure in people living with HIV. 12. Wu P and colleagues found that combining pill counts with self-reported adherence is a strong predictor of first-line ART failure in adults in South Africa. 13. Chammartin F et al. analyzed data from the International Epidemiology Databases to Evaluate AIDS (IeDEA) in sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on ART outcomes from 2012 to 2019. 14. Carlucci JG and colleagues examined the attrition of HIV-positive children from HIV services in lowand middle-income countries, identifying barriers to retention in care. 15. Frijters EM et al. identified risk factors for loss to follow-up in ART programs in lowand middle-income countries, providing insights into improving patient retention. 16. Penn AW and colleagues reviewed supportive interventions to improve ART retention in lowand middle-income countries, highlighting strategies to enhance care engagement. 17. Grimwood A et al. demonstrated that community adherence support improves program retention in children on ART in South Africa. 18. Luque-Fernandez MA et al. evaluated the effectiveness of patient adherence groups as a care model for stable ART patients in Cape Town, South Africa. 19. Zerbe A and colleagues piloted community-based adherence clubs for postpartum women on ART in Cape Town, South Africa, showing promising results for retention. 20. Munyayi FK and van Wyk B assessed the impact of Teen Clubs on retention in HIV care among adolescents in Namibia, highlighting the benefits of youth-focused interventions. 21. Braithstein P et al. proposed a clinician-nurse model to reduce early mortality and improve clinic retention among high-risk HIV-infected patients initiating ART. 22. Mfinanga S and colleagues evaluated cryptococcal meningitis screening and community-based early adherence support in people with advanced HIV infection in Tanzania and Zambia. 23. Hall BJ et al. conducted a qualitative meta-synthesis to identify barriers and facilitators to interventions aimed at improving retention in HIV care. 24. Geldsetzer P et al. systematically reviewed interventions to improve postpartum retention of women in PMTCT (prevention of mother-to-child transmission) and ART care. 25. Catalani C et al. reviewed the use of mHealth technologies for HIV treatment and prevention, highlighting their potential to improve care delivery. 26. Njoroge M et al. assessed the feasibility of eHealth and mHealth initiatives in Kenya, providing evidence for their implementation in resource-limited settings. 27. Nelson KM et al. reviewed mHealth interventions for HIV prevention and treatment among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men, emphasizing the role of technology in addressing this population's needs. 28. Maloney KM et al. systematically reviewed electronic and new media technology interventions for HIV care and prevention, demonstrating their effectiveness in improving outcomes. 29. WHO guidelines on HIV disclosure counseling for children up to 12 years of age provide recommendations for supporting families in managing disclosure. 30. Wolf HT et al. explored reasons for loss to follow-up among HIV-positive youth in Kenya, identifying stigma and social barriers as key factors. 31. WHO guidelines emphasize strategies to improve men's uptake of HIV testing and linkage to care services, addressing gender-specific barriers. 32. Zurcher K et al. analyzed outcomes of HIV-positive patients lost to follow-up in African treatment programs, providing insights into re-engagement strategies. 33. Mirzazadeh A et al. systematically reviewed interventions to re-engage people living with HIV who are lost to follow-up, offering evidence-based recommendations. 34. Li Y et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the association between intimate partner violence and HIV infection among women, highlighting the need for integrated interventions. 35. Sikazwe I et al. examined patient-reported reasons for stopping care or switching clinics in Zambia, using a multi-site, regionally representative approach. 36. Keene C et al. described Médecins Sans Frontières' Welcome Service, a collaborative reorganization of HIV services to address disengagement from care in South Africa. 37. Camlin CS et al. identified patient-reported factors associated with re-engagement in HIV care among disengaged patients in East Africa. 38. Amstutz A et al. evaluated engagement in care, viral suppression, and drug resistance following home-based same-day ART initiation in Lesotho. 39. Kredo T et al. reviewed task-shifting from doctors to non-doctors for ART initiation and maintenance, demonstrating its feasibility in resource-limited settings. 40. Mbeye NM et al. systematically reviewed task-shifting from pharmacy to non-pharmacy personnel for ART delivery, highlighting its potential to improve access. 41. Penazzato M et al. reviewed task-shifting for pediatric ART delivery, emphasizing its role in addressing workforce shortages. 42. Jaffar S et al. compared virological failure rates in home-based versus facility-based HIV care models in Uganda, demonstrating equivalence in outcomes. 43. Harries AD et al. proposed strategies to improve patient retention on ART in sub-Saharan Africa, addressing systemic and individual-level barriers. 44. Cometto G et al. provided WHO guidelines on optimizing community health worker programs to support HIV care delivery. 45. Vojnov L et al. reviewed the performance of non-laboratory staff in diagnostic testing and specimen collection in HIV programs, demonstrating their effectiveness. 46. Luo R et al. systematically reviewed the clinical impact of point-of-care early infant diagnosis for HIV, highlighting its potential to improve outcomes. 47. WHO guidelines on HIV testing services provide recommendations for improving access and quality of testing. 48. Luchters S et al. evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a low-cost, instrument-free point-of-care CD4 test among pregnant women, demonstrating its feasibility. 49. Ochodo E et al. reviewed point-of-care tests for detecting HIV nucleic acids in infants and children under 18 months, emphasizing their diagnostic value. 50. Adeloye D and Basquill C estimated the prevalence and awareness rates of hypertension in Africa, providing a systematic analysis of the burden. 51. Drain PK et al. validated a clinic-based cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay screening in HIV-infected adults in South Africa, demonstrating its accuracy. 52. Wake RM et al. showed that pipetting finger-prick blood improves the performance of cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assays. 53. Williams DA et al. evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a fingerstick cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay in HIV-infected individuals. 54. Olugbenga I et al. assessed the diagnostic accuracy of a dual rapid test for HIV and syphilis screening in pregnant women in Nigeria. 55. Gous N et al. demonstrated the feasibility of performing multiple point-of-care tests for ART initiation and monitoring using single or multiple fingersticks. 56. Jani IV et al. evaluated the accuracy of CD4 T-cell enumeration and ART toxicity monitoring using point-of-care testing in primary healthcare clinics. 57. Drain PK et al. combined point-of-care HIV viral load testing with task-shifting to improve treatment outcomes in a randomized controlled trial. 58. Le Roux S et al. systematically reviewed the clinical and operational impact of point-of-care versus laboratory-based nucleic acid testing for routine HIV viral load monitoring. 59. WHO guidelines summarize key features and recommendations for using antiretroviral drugs to treat and prevent HIV infection. 60. Haghigat R et al. reviewed the effects of decentralizing ART care delivery on health outcomes for adolescents and young adults in lowand middle-income countries. 61. Kredo T et al. reviewed the decentralization of HIV treatment in lowand middle-income countries, demonstrating its potential to improve access. 62. Ciapponi A et al. provided an overview of systematic reviews on delivery arrangements for health systems in low-income countries. 63. Lazarus JV et al. reviewed health service delivery models for ART provision in sub-Saharan Africa, identifying effective strategies for improving outcomes. 64. Duff P et al. identified barriers to accessing HAART among HIV-positive women attending antenatal clinics in Uganda, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions.
